items.q: The Ariane 5 disaster (1996) is cited as a quality lesson because:
options: A 64-bit float to 16-bit integer overflow crashed both primary and backup (identical software fails the same way)
The rocket ran out of fuel
items.explain: Reused Ariane-4 inertial software hit a 64→16-bit overflow on Ariane 5's higher velocity — in the backup AND then the primary. Redundant identical software fails identically: software is a single point of failure.

items.q: Which is NOT one of the six ISO 9126 quality characteristics?
items.explain: ISO 9126's six are Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability. Profitability is not one of them.

items.q: The IEEE 1061 definition says a software quality metric outputs:
options: A single numerical value interpreted as the degree to which the software possesses a quality attribute
items.explain: IEEE 1061: a quality metric is a function whose inputs are software data and whose output is a single numerical value interpreted as the degree to which the software possesses a given quality attribute.

items.q: Function Points measure software size based on:
options: The functional view — inputs, outputs, queries and files delivered to the user (language-independent)
items.explain: Function points count EI/EO/EQ/ILF/EIF adjusted for complexity, measuring functionality delivered to the end user — language-independent, unlike LOC.

items.q: In function point analysis, 'ILF' stands for:
items.explain: The five FP components: External Inputs (EI), External Outputs (EO), External Inquiries (EQ), Internal Logical Files (ILF, e.g. DB tables), External Interface Files (EIF, shared data sources).

items.q: Failure Rate, in the product-related test measures, is defined as:
options: The inverse of MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)
items.explain: Failure Rate = 1/MTBF. MTBF is a statistical measure of the probability of failure; its inverse is the failure rate.

items.q: Goodhart's Law states that:
options: More tests always mean fewer bugs
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
items.explain: Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' — people optimize the number, often by gaming it (e.g. Wells Fargo's 3.5M fake accounts).

items.q: The 'Coverage Paradox' warns that:
options: Coverage–effectiveness correlation is weak once test-suite size is controlled — diverse tests catch bugs, coverage is a side effect
items.explain: Studies found only low-to-moderate coverage–effectiveness correlation after controlling for suite size. It's diverse test cases (not the coverage %) that catch bugs; coverage is a side effect, not the cause.

items.q: An API with a 500ms average response time can still be problematic because:
options: The average can hide a long tail (e.g. 1% of requests at 30s) — use percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
items.explain: Averages hide tail latency — 95% at 200ms but 1% at 30s still averages ~500ms. Always report percentiles, not just the mean.

items.q: Open-Source Software is characterized by:
options: No source code, only a binary
Source-code availability plus the right to modify and (often) redistribute derivatives
Being always free of cost only
items.explain: OSS = source availability + right to modify/create derivatives + (often) redistribute them. Proprietary software is a 'black box' (binary only, EULA may prohibit reverse-engineering).

items.q: Stallman's four software freedoms describe 'free as in':
options: Free as in speech (liberties: run, study, redistribute, modify)
items.explain: 'Free as in speech, not as in beer' — the four freedoms (0: run, 1: study/change, 2: redistribute, 3: distribute modifications) are about liberties, not price.

items.q: In the 'Cathedral and the Bazaar', the Bazaar model refers to:
options: Centralized development by a core group, released when complete
Open, organic development with wide participation (e.g. Linux)
items.explain: Cathedral = centrally developed by a core group (GNU Emacs, GCC); Bazaar = developed openly/organically with wide participation (Linux). 'The Bazaar won.'

items.q: Which license is copyleft, requiring derivative works to use the same license?
items.explain: The GPL is copyleft: modifications must be relicensed under the GPL and source made available ('viral'). MIT, Apache and BSD are permissive.

items.q: The LGPL differs from the GPL in that it:
options: Allows proprietary code to depend on (dynamically link) the library without becoming GPL
items.explain: The LGPL (for libraries) does not treat dynamic binding as a derivative work, so proprietary code may depend on unmodified LGPL libraries — unlike the fully viral GPL.

items.q: Copyright vs Intellectual Property/Patents: copyright covers ___ while patents cover ___:
options: the particular expression of a work (and is automatic); ideas for solving a problem (and must be applied for)
items.explain: Copyright covers expressions (source code, books) and is automatic; patents/IP cover ideas for solving problems, must be applied for, and have expiry dates.

items.q: To be patentable, an invention must be:
items.explain: A patent requires the invention be New, Useful, and Non-obvious, with technical details disclosed publicly. It lasts 20 years.

items.q: A patent grants the holder the right to:
options: Make and sell the invention themselves
Exclude others from making, using, or selling the invention for the term
items.explain: A patent does NOT grant the right to make/use/sell; it grants the right to EXCLUDE others for the patent term (20 years) — enabling lawsuits, licensing, royalties.

items.q: A 'patent troll' (Non-Practicing Entity) is an organization that:
options: Acquires vague patents and sues others rather than making products
items.explain: Patent trolls (NPEs) don't build products; they hold vague patents and sue. Because US parties pay their own legal fees, it's often cheaper to settle than fight — a tax on innovation.

items.q: The four levels of testing, from smallest to largest scope, are:
items.explain: Unit (individual unit) → Integration (interfaces between components) → System (whole system) → Acceptance (does it meet user needs?).

items.q: In top-down integration, you need ___ to stand in for lower-level components not yet built:
items.explain: Top-down integration starts at the UI and works inward, needing stubs for lower levels. Bottom-up starts at data/logic layers and needs drivers to call them.

items.q: The 'sandwich' integration approach:
options: Connects top-level UI with crucial bottom components and adds middle layers incrementally (common, agile)
items.explain: Sandwich integration builds a skeleton: connect top-level UI with crucial bottom-level components, then add middle layers incrementally — the most common, agile approach.

items.q: Load testing vs stress testing: stress testing:
options: Applies extreme load to find the breaking point where the system fails
items.explain: Load testing applies the expected/above-average load; stress testing applies extreme load to determine the point at which the system breaks under high traffic.

items.q: System testing is characterized as:
options: Black-box, end-to-end testing of the completely integrated system against the SRS
items.explain: System testing is black-box, end-to-end testing of the fully integrated system for compliance with the Software Requirement Specification.

items.q: Release testing differs from system testing mainly in that release testing:
options: Is done by the dev team to find bugs
Is done by a separate team to validate the system is good enough for external use
items.explain: System testing (dev team) is defect testing — find bugs. Release testing (a separate, uninvolved team) is validation testing — confirm the system meets requirements and is good enough for external use.

items.q: Penetration testing is best described as:
options: An authorized, simulated cyberattack to find and exploit vulnerabilities before real attackers do
items.explain: Pentesting is an authorized, simulated attack using attacker tools/techniques to find and exploit vulnerabilities before real attackers, then report fixes.

items.q: In penetration testing, a 'black-box' test means the tester:
options: Has full source code and architecture
Knows only public information, like a real external attacker
items.explain: Black-box = only public info (best simulates an external attacker). White-box = full knowledge (most thorough). Gray-box = partial knowledge (hybrid).

items.q: Which is the correct order of the penetration-testing process?
options: Reconnaissance → Scanning → Vulnerability Assessment → Exploitation → Reporting
items.explain: The 5-phase process: Reconnaissance (gather info) → Scanning (ports/services) → Vulnerability Assessment (prioritize) → Exploitation (prove impact) → Reporting (findings + fixes).

items.q: Which open-source tool automates SQL injection discovery and exploitation?
items.explain: SQLMap automates SQL injection. Nmap = network scanner; OWASP ZAP = web DAST scanner; Wireshark = packet analyzer; Metasploit = exploitation framework.

items.q: Fuzzing is:
options: A static analysis of source code
Automated dynamic testing feeding random/malformed inputs to trigger crashes and memory errors
items.explain: Fuzzing is dynamic testing: feed random/malformed/unexpected inputs to trigger crashes, assertion failures, or memory errors — exploring thousands-millions of inputs.

items.q: A coverage-guided (gray-box) fuzzer like AFL works by:
options: Favoring inputs that exercise new code paths and mutating them further (feedback-driven)
items.explain: Coverage-guided fuzzers use feedback: inputs that hit new branches/coverage are 'favored' and mutated further, steering the fuzzer deeper into the code automatically.

items.q: A mutation-based fuzzer generates inputs by:
options: Building from a grammar/spec from scratch
Starting from valid sample inputs and modifying them (flip bits, alter lengths)
items.explain: Mutation-based fuzzers mutate valid seed inputs (flip bits, alter lengths). Generation-based fuzzers build new inputs from a model/grammar of the input format.

items.q: Google's OSS-Fuzz is notable for:
options: Continuously fuzzing thousands of open-source projects and finding ~10,000 bugs
items.explain: OSS-Fuzz continuously fuzzes thousands of open-source projects, reporting CVEs (e.g. the OpenSSL 2022 Punycode overflows) and finding ~10,000 bugs since launch.

items.q: A person-in-the-middle (PITM) attacker can:
options: Intercept traffic and both read AND change messages before forwarding them
items.explain: A PITM attacker intercepts network traffic and can read the messages and change them before sending them on (to the correct or incorrect destination).

items.q: The 'Big-3' of network security are:
items.explain: The Big-3: Authentication (who you're communicating with), Authorization (privilege to perform an operation), Confidentiality (communicate without others reading/changing it, incl. replay protection).

items.q: Which of the Big-3 protects against sniffing/eavesdropping?
items.explain: Confidentiality protects against sniffing (they can intercept, but can't read the content). Spoofing → Authentication; PITM → Authentication + Confidentiality.

items.q: Cumulative GDPR fines since 2018 (as cited) total roughly:
items.explain: Cumulative GDPR fines since 2018 ≈ €5.88 billion (Ireland alone ~€3.5B), including Meta €1.2B, Amazon €746M, TikTok €530M.

items.q: The two CORE principles of the FTC Fair Information Practice Principles are:
items.explain: FTC FIPPs: Notice/Awareness and Choice/Consent are the two CORE principles; the others are Access/Participation, Integrity/Security, and Enforcement.

items.q: Privacy-by-Design (PbD) means:
options: Adding privacy controls just before release
Building privacy in from the start, not bolting it on late
Collecting as much data as possible
items.explain: Privacy-by-Design builds privacy in from the start. Other mechanisms: selective collection, data minimization (pseudonymization/anonymization), retention policies, cryptography, threat modelling.

items.q: LINDDUN is a taxonomy of:
options: Privacy threats (Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance)
items.explain: LINDDUN is the privacy-threat taxonomy (mirror of security's STRIDE): Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure of information, Unawareness, Non-compliance.

items.q: Collecting phone numbers when email would suffice is which LINDDUN threat?
options: Disclosure of information (over-collection / lack of data minimization)
items.explain: Collecting more data than needed maps to Disclosure of information / poor data minimization in LINDDUN — the question 'are we collecting phone numbers when email would suffice?'

items.q: Statement, decision, and condition coverage differ; condition coverage requires that:
options: Every atomic condition takes both true and false at least once
items.explain: Statement coverage = every statement executed once; decision coverage = every decision both true & false; condition coverage = every ATOMIC condition both true & false.

items.q: A 'condition' (in coverage terminology) is:
options: An atomic boolean expression that cannot be decomposed into simpler boolean expressions
items.explain: A condition is an atomic boolean expression (can't be decomposed). A decision is a boolean expression composed of conditions joined by logical connectors.

items.q: How much code coverage does Google aim for, given diminishing returns?
options: Around 80%, focusing extra effort on high-risk code
items.explain: 100% is subject to diminishing returns (the last 10% can need 50% more test code). Google aims for ~80%, documents exceptions, and focuses on high-risk code (security, payments, data).

items.q: A key limitation of code coverage is that:
options: It is not sufficient to ensure correctness (you can have high coverage with wrong outputs or missing requirements)
items.explain: Coverage shows what code ran, not whether outputs are correct or whether required code is missing. It's a guide to test adequacy, not a proof of correctness.

items.q: The Volkswagen emissions scandal involved engineers who:
options: Deliberately wrote a 'defeat device' that detected emissions tests and ran clean only during them
items.explain: VW engineers wrote code that detected when the car was being emissions-tested, running clean during tests but emitting up to 40x the legal limit on the road — $30B in fines and criminal charges.

items.q: The Twitter photo-cropping case illustrates the principle that:
options: Intent doesn't excuse impact — bias from biased data and no fairness testing still causes harm
items.explain: The engineers didn't intend a racist algorithm, but trained on biased data, didn't test for fairness, and deployed to millions. Intent doesn't excuse impact.

items.q: A notable research finding about codes of ethics is that:
options: They do not appear to change the decisions software developers actually make
They replace the need for laws
items.explain: Research shows the code of ethics does not appear to affect developers' actual decisions — knowing principles isn't enough; ethics must be practised and reinforced.

items.q: The three 'human flourishing' questions to ask of your software include all EXCEPT:
options: Does it respect the humanity of the users?
Does it amplify positive or negative behavior?
Will its quality impact the humanity of others?
items.explain: The three questions: (1) respect users' humanity? (2) amplify positive or negative behavior? (3) will quality impact others' humanity? Maximizing ad revenue is not one of them.
